title: Behind Google's AI Exodus: Hassabis Planned Exit for a Year as Model Delays Fueled Departures
excerpt: New reporting reveals the DeepMind CEO had been seeking a return to pure science for months, while unreleased Gemini models and rival poaching accelerated the biggest AI talent drain in tech history.
body:
• Demis Hassabis had been discussing his exit from the DeepMind CEO role for at least a year, seeking to refocus on scientific research and his drug discovery company Isomorphic Labs.
  • Google's flagship Gemini 3.5 Pro model remains unreleased after three missed targets since its planned June launch, with persistent shortcomings in coding and reasoning capabilities.
  • Discovery Loop, co-founded by four departing veterans including Rajasthan-born Sanjay Ghemawat, has secured backing from Alphabet, Radical Ventures, Khosla Ventures, Kleiner Perkins, and Lightspeed.
  • Six senior AI leaders have departed Google since June, with combined exits erasing roughly $300 billion from Alphabet's market value.

A week after Google's most significant AI leadership restructuring in years, new reporting has revealed the internal dynamics that drove the departures — from a Nobel laureate's year-long quest to return to pure science, to mounting frustration over delayed model releases and a steady loss of top researchers to OpenAI and Anthropic.

A Year in the Making

The departure of Demis Hassabis from the Google DeepMind CEO role was anything but sudden. Sources familiar with his thinking told Semafor that the Nobel Prize recipient had been contemplating the switch for at least a year, gradually reducing his involvement with consumer AI products while chief technology officer Koray Kavukcuoglu quietly assumed more operational duties.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=VJDxypU66PU

Hassabis, who co-founded DeepMind in 2010 and continued running it after Google's $650 million acquisition in 2014, had grown increasingly focused on Isomorphic Labs, the Alphabet drug discovery spinoff he founded and still leads as CEO. The company raised $2.1 billion in May, fueling his push to apply AI to pharmaceutical breakthroughs rather than chatbot competition.

"I've always believed the No. 1 application of AI should be to improve human health. It's time for AI to prove its unequivocal value to the world, and what better way to demonstrate that than to help finally cure diseases like cancer."

— Demis Hassabis, in a company memo

In his new role as Alphabet's chief scientist and DeepMind chairman, Hassabis will have few direct reports and will focus on AGI strategy and Isomorphic Labs, leaving the operational challenge to Kavukcuoglu.

Gemini Delays Fan the Flames

The timing of the reshuffle was no coincidence. Google's flagship Gemini 3.5 Pro model remains unreleased despite being announced at Google I/O in May with a June launch target. Internal testing reportedly uncovered persistent shortcomings in coding capabilities and mathematical reasoning — the very areas where Anthropic and OpenAI have built commanding leads.

The delay marked the third missed deadline for the model, and it landed during a period when Google was already losing senior talent at an alarming rate. Noam Shazeer, co-author of the seminal 2017 transformer paper "Attention Is All You Need" and co-lead of Gemini development, departed for OpenAI in June. John Jumper, who shared the 2024 Nobel Prize with Hassabis for the AlphaFold protein-folding breakthrough, left for Anthropic the same week. Together, those departures triggered a 5% single-session drop in Alphabet shares, erasing roughly $225 billion in market value.

Discovery Loop and the Pull of Independence

Jeff Dean's exit after 27 years — taking three decorated colleagues with him — compounded the market rout. Dean, Google's 30th employee and co-founder of Google Brain, launched Discovery Loop alongside Sanjay Ghemawat, Oriol Vinyals, and Quoc Le. The public benefit corporation aims to automate the entire scientific research process: proposing experiments, building infrastructure, running tests, evaluating results, and iterating — a cycle that typically runs thousands of times before yielding a discovery.

Ghemawat, who grew up in Kota, Rajasthan, spent nearly three decades at Google building foundational technologies including Google File System, MapReduce, and Bigtable. He offered the clearest account of why the group left: Google's infrastructure works well for consumer apps, ads, and search, he told The Wall Street Journal, but has "very different requirements" than what scientific research demands.

"It is just a very different environment inside a startup. It is much more fast-paced and focused. You are a smaller team. There is much less bureaucracy and politics."

— Tim Rocktäschel, former Google researcher

Discovery Loop has secured investment from Alphabet — which will also serve as its cloud partner, providing first-year computing capacity — with Radical Ventures and Khosla Ventures co-leading a seed round that includes Kleiner Perkins, Lightspeed, and Doerr Capital.

Indian-Origin Leaders at the Center

The restructuring underscores the outsized role of Indian-origin talent in shaping the global AI landscape. Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, born in Chennai, is navigating the most consequential leadership transition of his tenure. Ghemawat carries his Rajasthan roots from the company's foundational era into a startup aimed at accelerating scientific discovery. The Gemini team they built together now falls to Kavukcuoglu, who faces the challenge of delivering results while competing for researchers against some of the richest AI startups in history.

What Comes Next

Google retains significant structural advantages: its TPU hardware ecosystem, massive compute infrastructure, and the Gemini app's 950 million monthly users. Pichai has emphasized that Alphabet is "committed to being at the frontier" and remains "super focused on the areas where we need to improve."

But the new operational leader inherits an uphill race against OpenAI and Anthropic, a delayed flagship model, a depleted senior bench, and a company that turned free cash flow negative for the first time in its public history last quarter while forecasting up to $205 billion in capital expenditures. Whether Google can reverse the talent drain may depend on how quickly Gemini 3.5 Pro finally ships — and whether it delivers capabilities that justify the wait.
